Subject: SLA anchors + monthly remedy ask

Laura —

Thanks for the call earlier. To recap Finex's ask: we need a clear, conservative SLA anchor for hosted inference that we can present to our legal/procurement teams. Specifically: a standard uptime floor for the service (we're thinking 99.90% as an initial baseline), a p95 latency floor for generation routes (target below 500ms in our primary region), and a predictable monthly credit mechanism if targets aren't met.

Two clarifying points from procurement:
- We need a cap on monthly credits (cannot be open-ended).
- Regional carveouts matter to us (EU vs US availability should be separable).

Can you propose a short, commercial-friendly template that shows: uptime tiers, how monthly credits are calculated, an example month with sample numbers, and typical carveouts (scheduled maintenance, force majeure, planned capacity increases)? If you can attach a one-page worked example, that would help shorten our internal review.

Appreciate it — Evan

--

Evan — thanks for the clear summary. Passing a first-pass template and a short worked example (attached). High-level proposal below, then attachments.

Quick commercial summary (proposed):
- Uptime anchor: 99.95% for dedicated customers, 99.90% for standard hosted tier.
- Monthly remedy: pro-rata token-credit model where each minute of aggregated monthly downtime below the anchor converts to a token credit at a published rate; monthly cap = 20% of monthly invoice for hosted customers (negotiable for enterprise).
- Latency: p95 generation latency SLA of <500ms for <4k context single-stream routes in primary region; remediation for repeated monthly p95 breaches limited to configuration credits (beyond uptime credits).
- Regional model: availability measured per-region; credits calculated per-region and aggregated with an upper cap.
- Common carveouts: scheduled maintenance (with 48h notice and <6h/mo allowance), force majeure, and customer-caused outages.

Attachments: Redwood_SLA_Draft_v2.pdf (one-page commercial summary + legal-friendly wording) and sla_calculation_example.xlsx (worked example with a sample month showing calculations and cap enforcement).

If acceptable, next step would be: 1) Procurement confirms cap tolerance (20% is our standard ask fallback), and 2) we send a redline-friendly clause set for their legal team.

Best,

Looping in a couple of commercial guardrails from my side — feel free to fold this into the draft.

Notes / alternate framing we usually find helpful when negotiating with finance/procurement:
- Cap structure: instead of a percent of invoice, propose a tiered cap that scales with ARR band (e.g., up to $50k/mo -> cap 25%; $50k–250k -> cap 15%; >$250k -> cap 10%). This gives procurement certainty while protecting economics for high-commitment customers.
- Graceband: offer a 1-month lookback smoothing option so a one-off incident doesn't immediately trigger full remediation — achieves a balance between reliability and noisy months.
- Latency remediation: prefer non-monetary remedies (engineering time credits, prioritized triage) unless the customer is on a dedicated SLA. For hosted customers keep it to configuration credits to avoid open-ended payouts.

I'll add a short paragraph to the draft PDF suggesting the tiered cap table; Laura if you want I can push an updated PDF with the tiered caps.

— Ben

Technical notes to anchor the commercial language so we don't promise things we can't measurably deliver: 

- Measurement windows: uptime measured as the percentage of successful API availability per-region per-calendar month, using our telemetry (internal service-side pings + customer-visible synthetic checks). Define a 5-minute min incident granularity.
- Maintenance allowance: suggest we codify a 6-hour scheduled maintenance allowance per month per-region (with 48h notice). That sits better with our planned kernel/driver updates and batching optimization rollouts.
- Latency caveats: <500ms p95 is realistic for light-generation routes; for heavy multi-stream or long-context batches P95 will vary — recommend adding an explicit clause that defines route classes and their baseline test harness.
- Calculation example: in the attached spreadsheet I modeled a 30-day month, showed how a 3-hour outage in us-west reduces uptime and translates to credits under both the % cap and Ben's tiered cap example.

If procurement wants tighter EU measurement, we can propose a separate regional SLA appendix (adds measurement and invoicing complexity but is doable).

—Marissa

Thanks — this is helpful and close to what procurement needs. A few quick requests before we move to redlines: 

1) For the tiered cap table Ben suggested, can you show a worked example in the spreadsheet for at least one mid-sized band (your sample did the top-end). We want to show our CFO a clear worst-case payout for a 3-hour outage.
2) Please include the DocuSign-ready clause text (we prefer copy-paste text for our contract team).
3) Can you confirm the notification & incident reporting SLA (how we get alerted and expected investigation timelines)?

If you can send an updated PDF with the tiered cap example and a DocuSign clause, procurement can usually turn it around in 48–72 hours.

Evan
